summary: Teach ratio notation as meaning before manipulation: a:b means 'for every a there are b', with order fixed to the wording (boys:girls written boys-first). Simplify by dividing BOTH parts by a common factor, reaching simplest form only when no common factor other than 1 remains (equivalently, once the parts have been divided by their highest common factor). Convert to fractions of the whole using the TOTAL of the parts as the denominator (3:2 means 3/5 and 2/5, not 3/2). Handle decimal or fraction ratios by first scaling up to whole numbers. The core insight is that simplifying keeps the SAME relationship with smaller numbers (an equivalent ratio).
misconceptions: Stops before simplest form — divides by a common factor but not the HCF (12:8 → 6:4 and leaves it)
Reverses the order relative to the wording (writes girls:boys)
Converts a:b to fractions using the other part as the denominator (3:2 → 3/2) instead of the whole (3/5)
Simplifies by subtracting a constant from both parts (12:8 → 4:0 or 11:7) rather than dividing — an additive slip

activities.title: Ratio simplifying bench with a shape-stays-the-same check
steps: Enter a ratio such as 12:8 and simplify it by repeatedly choosing a number to divide BOTH parts by (e.g. ÷4 straight to 3:2, or ÷2 to 6:4 then ÷2 again).
Watch two scaled bars drawn beside the numbers: as 12:8 becomes 6:4 becomes 3:2, the bars keep the same shape/proportion, showing the relationship is preserved.

Use a 'can this go smaller?' indicator that stays red while a common factor greater than 1 still divides both parts and turns green only when none does, so 'simplest form' becomes a testable end-state.
Then snap the 3 and 2 blocks together into one whole of 5 and read off the part-to-whole fractions 3/5 and 2/5 from the total number of blocks.
For a decimal or fraction ratio (0.5:2, or 1/2:1/3), first apply a scale-up step (×2, ×10, or a common multiplier) to reach whole numbers (0.5:2 → 1:4; 1/2:1/3 → 3:2), then simplify.
activities.insight: Simplifying a ratio keeps the same 'for every' relationship with smaller numbers; simplest form means no common factor remains; and converting to a fraction uses the whole (a+b) as the denominator.

activities.title: Scored practice set with targeted ratio errors
steps: Fill in the blanks to simplify: 12:8 = ☐:☐ (expecting 3:2 in simplest form).
Match several ratios (12:8, 6:4, 9:6) to their shared simplest form 3:2.

Choose what fraction of the whole the first part of 3:2 represents, from options including 3/5 (correct), 3/2 (the part-to-part comparison read as a fraction) and 2/5 (the other part's share of the whole).
activities.insight: Fluent writing, simplifying and converting of ratios, with the common errors made explicit through the wrong-answer options offered.

activities.title: Verbal coaching of the simplest-form check
steps: Work through one ratio aloud with a prompt such as 'Can both numbers be divided again?' at each step until no common factor remains.
State why 4:0 (from subtracting) cannot be a valid simplification: it would mean 'no girls', which changes the relationship.
activities.insight: Simplest form is reached only when no factor divides both parts, and simplifying must preserve the 'for every' relationship (divide, do not subtract).

activities.title: Worked simplify-and-convert reference
steps: Reveal, on a fixed example, that 12:8 divides by 4 to give 3:2.
Reveal on the bar for 3:2 that there are 5 equal parts, so the fractions of the whole are 3/5 and 2/5.
activities.insight: A single clear chain from a ratio to its simplest form and then to fractions of the whole, available as a reference model.

checkQuestion: In a class there are 12 boys and 8 girls. Write the ratio of boys to girls, then simplify it as far as it will go. After that, tell me what fraction of the whole class are boys. Do it however you like — I'll watch, you don't need to explain the rule.
checkAnswer: Ratio 12:8, simplified to 3:2 (dividing both by the HCF 4). Boys are 3 out of the 5 equal parts, so 3/5 of the class.
